text:
Keep the Joins: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years a headline announces the death of cursive. Keyboards have won, the argument goes, so children should not waste precious classroom hours looping their letters together. Some education systems have already acted on this logic. Several American states dropped cursive from their standards, and teachers elsewhere quietly let it slide. I think this is a mistake. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it properly, because it serves children in ways that a keyboard does not and cannot.

Start with the claim that handwriting is obsolete. It is not. Children sit exams by hand. They write notes in lessons, fill in forms, label diagrams, sign their names, and scribble shopping lists and birthday cards. Even in the most screen-saturated classroom, a pen or pencil remains the fastest and most flexible tool for a quick thought. A child who cannot write fluently by hand is a child who is slowed down in nearly every subject, every day. The question is therefore not whether children will handwrite, but whether they will do it well or badly. Joined-up writing is the best route to doing it well.

The case rests first on fluency. Printed letters require the pen to lift after every stroke. Each lift is a small interruption, and each restart is a new chance to misjudge size, spacing or direction. Joined writing replaces many of those restarts with a continuous movement. The hand develops a rhythm, and the word becomes a single gesture rather than a string of separate drawings. Once a child masters the join, speed rises without the mess that usually comes from rushing. Teachers who have watched a class move from laboured printing to confident flow know how large the change can be. A child who writes quickly and legibly can keep up with her own thinking, and that matters enormously for the quality of what she produces.

That brings me to the second argument, which concerns cognitive load. Writing is hard for young children. They must hold the sentence in mind, recall the spelling, form each letter, and manage the page, all at once. Anything that makes the physical act cheaper leaves more attention for the content. Research on early writing has repeatedly found that children whose handwriting is automatic write longer, more ambitious pieces than those still struggling to form letters. Automaticity is the goal, and a fluent joined script is one of the surest ways to reach it. A child who no longer has to think about her pencil can think instead about her story.

Third, there is the evidence on how handwriting shapes learning itself. Studies comparing handwriting with typing, including work using brain imaging with children and adults, have found that forming letters by hand activates reading and language regions more strongly than pressing keys does. Young children who practise writing letters freehand recognise them more readily than those who only type or trace. The movement of the hand leaves a trace in memory. Typing, by contrast, offers every letter as an identical press of an identical key, so the body learns almost nothing about letter shape. Some of this research concerns print rather than cursive, and honesty requires me to say so. But it does establish the broader point that the motor act of writing helps thinking and memory, and joined writing is the most developed form of that act.

Critics will say that if handwriting matters, print will do. Print is perfectly legible, they note, and easier to learn. There is something in this. Many adults print happily, and no one should pretend that a joined script is a moral achievement. But the argument undersells what children gain from the extra step. Learning to join letters teaches control. It demands planning of the whole word before the pen moves, attention to slope and spacing, and the patient repetition of a fine motor pattern. These are valuable habits in themselves, and they transfer. A child who has practised steady, controlled movement is better prepared for drawing, for music, for sport and for any task that rewards a careful hand.

There is also a practical argument from spelling. Because a joined word is written as one movement, the child builds a physical memory of common letter strings such as ing, tion and ough. The hand learns the pattern even where the mind is unsure. Teachers often observe that children who join their writing spell familiar words more consistently, and the explanation is plausible. Muscle memory supports visual memory. Printing letter by letter does not give the same chunking of the word into a flowing whole.

Fourth, consider access to the past. Cursive is how most of our written history was made. Letters from grandparents, diaries, wartime postcards, school reports and family recipes are written in joined script. A child who cannot read cursive is cut off from these documents, or must rely on someone else to decode them. Reading joined writing is a skill in its own right, and the surest way to acquire it is to learn to produce it. Children who write cursive can read it. Children who never learn it often find a grandparent's handwriting as opaque as a foreign alphabet. That would be a strange loss to accept for the sake of a few saved lessons.

Fifth, and perhaps most important, is equity. Wealthy families will always find a way to teach their children to write beautifully, with calligraphy classes, tutors and plenty of practice at home. If schools abandon joined writing, they hand that advantage entirely to those households. Meanwhile the children who most need a clear, fast, reliable hand, those who struggle with literacy or who have no quiet place to practise at home, will be left with whatever they happened to pick up. Handwriting is a skill that school is uniquely well placed to teach, because it needs daily guided practice from a trained adult. Removing it from the curriculum does not abolish the need, it merely shifts the burden onto families, and the burden will fall unevenly.

What of the objection that time is scarce? Primary teachers face an overcrowded curriculum, and every minute spent on handwriting is a minute not spent on reading, mathematics or science. This is a fair concern, and I would not defend long, dull drills. But the time cost is modest. Ten or fifteen minutes a day, a few times a week, over a couple of years, is enough for most children to reach a fluent joined hand. In exchange, the whole of the rest of the curriculum gets easier to write about. Few investments of classroom time pay back so widely. If time is the problem, the answer is to teach handwriting efficiently, not to drop it.

The strongest version of the opposing view is that typing deserves the time instead, since children will type far more as adults. I agree that keyboard skills should be taught, and taught early. But this is not a competition. The two skills do different jobs. Typing is excellent for long documents, editing and sharing. Handwriting is better for note taking, for working through a problem, for exams, and for the many occasions when no device is at hand or permitted. A well-educated adult needs both, and the early primary years, when small hands are developing control, are exactly the right moment for the manual skill. Keyboards can be learned later and learned quickly. Fine motor patterns laid down in childhood are harder to acquire afterwards.

I should also say what good teaching of joined writing looks like, because the policy is only as good as its practice. Children should begin with print and move to joining once their letter formation is secure, usually around seven. Teachers should model the movements, watch posture and pencil grip, and give short, frequent practice rather than occasional long sessions. Schools should accept that some children, especially those with motor difficulties, will need support or a modified approach, and nobody should be shamed for untidy writing. The aim is a legible, comfortable, reasonably quick hand, not copperplate perfection. A child with a personal but fluent joined style has succeeded.

The strongest reason of all is also the simplest. Handwriting is one of the few things school teaches that a child can do alone, anywhere, with almost no equipment, for the rest of her life. It needs no battery, no signal and no subscription. It lets her think on paper, record what matters, and leave a mark that is recognisably her own. Joined-up writing is the most efficient and most expressive form of that skill. To remove it from primary schools because keyboards exist would be like abandoning mental arithmetic because calculators exist. Both tools have their place, but the older skill trains the mind in ways the newer one does not.

So the answer is yes. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. They should do it briskly, kindly and well, and they should treat it as what it is: a foundation for fluent thought, not a relic of a vanished age. The pen is not obsolete. It is simply the first tool a child learns to think with, and we should not take it away just when she is learning to use it.
